title: We've Been Studying System 1 All Along
author: Science of Explanation
summary: This article argues that the cognitive science of explanation has been studying System 1 — fast, automatic, pre-rational thinking — all along, even before Kahneman named and formalized it. Using the classic Linda Problem as its anchor, the author shows how people reason from the meaning or gist they construct from information rather than from information directly, leading to systematic and predictable errors even among educated adults. The piece situates the Linda Problem within Kahneman's landmark distinction between System 1 (fast, automatic) and System 2 (rational, effortful) thinking, arguing that this framework is the most important tool available for thinking about how information travels in the mind and how explanations succeed or fail. The article frames itself as foundational to a longer series on the science of explanation: understanding System 1's default dominance is the prerequisite for designing explanations that actually land. The piece takes a notable pedagogical stance — that people do not reason from information but from the meaning they construct — with significant implications for how teachers should structure explanations.
points: The Linda Problem reveals a fundamental feature of human cognition: we do not reason directly from information, we reason from the meaning (gist) we construct from that information. A vivid story about Linda makes Option B feel right even though it violates a basic law of probability.

Between 85 and 90% of participants in Kahneman's experiments chose the conjunction (Linda as bank teller AND feminist activist) over the simpler option, demonstrating that even educated adults systematically favour narrative coherence over logical validity.

Kahneman's System 1 / System 2 framework is presented as the most useful conceptual tool for understanding how explanations travel in the mind: System 1 (fast, automatic, pre-rational) is the default that processes most of what we encounter; System 2 (rational, effortful) must be deliberately activated.

The science of explanation has, in effect, always been studying System 1 — the conditions under which pre-rational processing leads us toward understanding or away from it. This reframe connects cognitive science directly to practical pedagogy.

Context and gist shape our thinking at every level: the compelling story of Linda's activist past primes System 1 to supply the answer that feels right, bypassing System 2's probabilistic logic entirely. Effective explanations must anticipate this dynamic.
quotes: Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken, and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations. 85% to 90% of participants chose Option B. It appears to make logical sense. But it's a mistake.

The probability of two events occurring together can never be greater than the probability of one of the events occurring alone. The Linda Problem shows that people do not reason directly from information; we reason from the meaning we construct from that information.

We quickly think: 'Linda is an outspoken activist, therefore it's more probable that she's a feminist bank teller.' The mistake feels reasonable because the description of Linda creates a compelling story. Rather than evaluating probability directly, we rely on the gist we formed from the details.

System 1: Immediate, automatic, pre-rational (fast). System 2: Rational, effortful, logical (slow). This framing provides a powerful way to think about the science of explanation and the gauntlet of the mind.

Kahneman showed that these errors happen in a wide variety of situations. We constantly rely on rapid judgments to make sense of the world, and while they are often useful, they can also lead us astray in predictable ways.
